title: Xcode compilation caching with Depot Cache
summary: Depot Cache now supports Xcode compilation caching. Reuse outputs across CI builds to reduce build times, with no extra setup on Depot runners.
body_markdown:
At Depot, we feel the need... the need for speed. That’s why we added support for Xcode compilation caching, a build feature introduced in Xcode 26. Let’s take a look at how it works and how you can make the most of it.


## How Xcode compilation caching works


Under the hood, Xcode’s compilation caching is built on[LLVM’s](https://llvm.org/docs/ContentAddressableStorage.html) Content Addressable Storage (CAS): an immutable store where every blob is addressed by a hash of its own content. Pair that with an action cache that maps “these exact inputs” to “this exact output”, and you’ve got a compiler that doesn’t have to redo work it has already done.


Before compiling a file, Xcode hashes everything that could affect the result, such as the source, its headers, the compiler flags and the toolchain version. That hash becomes the cache key, and it’s deterministic. Identical inputs always produce the same key. If the key is already in the cache, the compiler skips the work and pulls the finished output straight from the CAS.


### Connecting Xcode to Depot Cache


And since everything is addressed by hash, the cache doesn’t have to live on your machine. This is where Depot Cache steps in. Apple’s LLVM fork defines a[gRPC](https://github.com/swiftlang/llvm-project/tree/next/llvm/lib/RemoteCachingService/RemoteCacheProto) protocol for talking to a remote CAS and action cache, and we implemented it on our side. Xcode asks Depot Cache whether it has seen this exact compilation before. If it has, the output comes back over the wire instead of being rebuilt. If it hasn’t, the fresh result gets uploaded so the next build can use it.


With caching turned on, Xcode first checks the local cache for an already compiled result, then asks the remote cache, and only falls back to an expensive compile if both come up empty. When it does have to compile, the output is stored in the CAS under its content hash, and the cache key is mapped to it, both locally and remotely. The next build on a Depot runner gets to skip the work.


If this reminds you of Bazel or Gradle, you’re not imagining things. Bazel’s remote cache uses the same pairing of a CAS and an action cache, and Gradle’s build cache runs on a similar idea. That is exactly why we could reuse the KV cache backend we’d already built for our other cache products, and why you get the same visibility and user experience you’re used to from them.


The big difference from Bazel is the price of admission. Getting real value out of Bazel usually means restructuring your project and changing how your team works. Compilation caching, on the other hand, works almost out of the box: change a couple of settings and point Xcode at Depot Cache, and you are good to go.


Xcode compilation cache during a build


## Using Xcode compilation caching with Depot


As with the rest of Depot Cache, compilation caching is on by default for builds using Xcode 26 or newer on Depot macOS runners. No setup required: we generate an xcconfig file at` /var/run/depot-xcode-cache.xcconfig` that layers the caching settings on top of your project’s own build configuration.


For workflow examples and configuration details, see the[Xcode compilation caching docs](https://depot.dev/docs/cache/integrations/xcode) .


Here are the keys we set:


```text
// Turns on compilation caching (sets SWIFT_ENABLE_COMPILE_CACHE and CLANG_ENABLE_COMPILE_CACHE under the hood)
COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING  =  YES
// Loads the plugin that lets the build system talk to an external cache service
COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_PLUGIN  =  YES
// Runs remote cache key lookups asynchronously, in parallel with the rest of the build
COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_DETACHED_KEY_QUERIES  =  YES
// Sends cache queries to the external cache service instead of the local cache
COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_INTEGRATED_QUERIES  =  YES
// Runs the Swift driver inside the build system instead of as a separate process, cutting inter-process overhead
SWIFT_USE_INTEGRATED_DRIVER  =  YES
// Imports system headers as Clang modules instead of raw textual includes, which speeds up builds and indexing
CLANG_ENABLE_MODULES  =  YES
// Remaps absolute SDK and toolchain paths to stable placeholders,
// so the same inputs produce the same cache key on every machine.
SWIFT_ENABLE_PREFIX_MAPPING  =  $  (  inherited  )
// Remaps the project directory to a stable placeholder,
// so the same code produces the same cache key no matter where the repo is checked out
SWIFT_ENABLE_PROJECT_PREFIX_MAPPING  =  YES
// Same as SWIFT_ENABLE_PREFIX_MAPPING, for C-family languages
CLANG_ENABLE_PREFIX_MAPPING  =  YES
// Same as SWIFT_ENABLE_PROJECT_PREFIX_MAPPING, for C-family languages
CLANG_ENABLE_PROJECT_PREFIX_MAPPING  =  YES
// Languages whose compile tasks use the remote cache
COMPILATION_CACHE_REMOTE_SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES   =   swift c c  ++   objective  -  c objective  -  c  ++
// Placeholders for build products, intermediates, the SDK stat cache and the home directory
DEPOT_XCODE_CACHE_PREFIX_MAPPINGS  =  $  (  SYMROOT  )  =  /^  symroot $  (  OBJROOT  )  =  /^  objroot $  (  SDK_STAT_CACHE_DIR  )  =  /^  dd $  (  HOME  )  =  /^  home
// Adds Depot's path mappings on top of any the project already defines
SWIFT_OTHER_PREFIX_MAPPINGS   =   $  (  inherited  )   $  (  DEPOT_XCODE_CACHE_PREFIX_MAPPINGS  )
CLANG_OTHER_PREFIX_MAPPINGS   =   $  (  inherited  )   $  (  DEPOT_XCODE_CACHE_PREFIX_MAPPINGS  )
```


One setting we deliberately leave alone is` SWIFT_ENABLE_PREFIX_MAPPING` . Forcing it on can break some projects, so we inherit whatever your project already uses. If your build works with it enabled, set it to` YES` and you’ll likely see a nice bump in cache hits.


We only touch the settings listed above. Everything else comes straight from your project’s configuration. If you need to change a setting, build settings passed on the` xcodebuild` command line take precedence over the Depot configuration.


To disable Depot’s Xcode compilation caching for a single build:


```text
xcodebuild   -scheme   MyApp   COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO   build
```


You can also opt out of compilation caching at any time by setting` DEPOT_XCODE_CACHE_ENABLED` to` 0` at the job or workflow level:


```text
env  :
DEPOT_XCODE_CACHE_ENABLED  :   0
```


## Track your cache performance


Xcode doesn’t provide cache statistics out of the box, which leaves you without much insight into how well the cache is performing. To address that, we built the` depot/xcode-compilation-cache-summary` action. Add it to your workflow *after* the step that runs` xcodebuild` , and at the end of the job it prints your cache statistics and adds them to the job summary. Here’s an example of the output:


```text
Depot Xcode compilation cache
Hits        5310
Misses      0
Hit rate    100.0%
Downloaded  2.2 GB
Uploaded    0 objects, 0 B
```

Enough talk, let’s see what the cache does for some real-world projects.


Overview of the Xcode build speed increase with Depot Cache


On top of that, one other customer with a fairly large iOS project reported a 40% reduction in build time, and that's without` SWIFT_ENABLE_PREFIX_MAPPING` turned on! 🎉


## One caveat


Compilation caching comes with one small caveat. If` DerivedData` is already populated when the build starts, Xcode uses what it finds there, and might not use Depot Cache at all. If your workflow restores` DerivedData` , we recommend removing that step when using compilation caching.


## Let us know how it goes


We’re determined to make our macOS offering best-in-class, and compilation caching is just one step on that road. We hope it takes a serious bite out of your build times. If it does,[let us know](https://discord.gg/depot) how much faster your workflow got.
